analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare offer its own prescription drug plan and negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: A bill to create a Medicare-run prescription drug plan with government-negotiated prices and a $35 monthly premium, backed by 6 Democratic senators, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a government-run prescription drug plan to Medicare's Part D program, offered nationwide alongside private drug plans. It would have required the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers to lower drug prices, and set a uniform national premium of $35 a month for 2006, with a guaranteed plan at that price. This directly challenged the 2003 Medicare law's structure, which relies entirely on private insurers and bars the government from negotiating drug prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — seniors and people with disabilities enrolled in Part D — would have gained a nationally uniform, lower-cost drug plan option with premiums set at $35 a month in 2006 and drug prices negotiated by the government rather than left to private insurers. The bill also encouraged steering patients to cheaper therapeutically equivalent drugs where medically appropriate. Taxpayers could have benefited if negotiated prices lowered Medicare's overall drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicare-operated prescription drug plan offered nationwide, in addition to the private Part D plans, giving beneficiaries a public option.

Directs the HHS Secretary to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers to reduce the purchase cost of covered Part D drugs, overriding the existing provision that bars the government from intervening in private plan negotiations.
Sets a uniform national monthly premium of $35 for 2006 and requires that at least one Medicare-operated plan be available at that price, replacing the varied regional premiums of private plans.
Requires the plan to encourage use of more affordable therapeutic equivalents, so long as that does not override a prescribing physician's judgment of medical necessity.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would have received lower negotiated prices on Medicare-covered drugs, and private insurers offering Part D plans would have lost enrollees and premiums to a cheaper government-run competitor. The bill also allows Medicare to make payments for the operating expenses of the government-run plans, so any shortfall between the $35 premium and actual costs could have fallen on taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private drug-plan insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill only directs the Secretary to 'negotiate' with manufacturers — it does not give the government authority to set prices or require companies to participate, so it is uncertain how much price reduction negotiation alone would actually produce.

A single nationally uniform premium of $35 for 2006 may not have matched actual costs everywhere, and since the bill authorizes Medicare payments for the plan's operating expenses, any gap between premiums and costs could have become a federal expense.

A government-run plan competing on price with private insurers could have drawn enrollees away from private Part D plans and shrunk or eliminated that market, the main objection insurers and drug makers raised to public-plan competition in Medicare.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If government negotiation had produced meaningful price cuts, beneficiaries would have gained a cheaper, simpler, nationally uniform drug plan, and the cost would have been borne mostly by drug manufacturers' Medicare revenue and private insurers' market share. The main weakness is the bill's own design: it relies on negotiation without giving the Secretary any authority to set prices or walk away from a deal, so the projected savings were speculative, and a below-cost $35 premium could have quietly shifted costs onto the federal budget.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it quietly died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on February 10, 2005, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
Five Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors.
Durbin gave introductory remarks on the bill again on September 27, 2005, but the Finance Committee took no further action.
No committee vote, floor vote, or hearing ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: the 2003 law's ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices stayed in place for another Congress, and private insurers kept the Part D market without a government-run competitor. Beneficiaries never got the lower-priced public plan option.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and Part D insurers

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor twice, in February and September 2005.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill, leaving it to die in committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed Medicare price negotiation, which the 2003 Medicare law they had shaped explicitly prohibited; the industry campaigned against letting the government negotiate drug prices.

against.name: Private health insurers offering Part D plans
against.what_they_did: Opposed a government-run drug plan that would compete with their products for Medicare beneficiaries.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; the Republican-run Finance Committee simply declined to act on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required the government to negotiate drug prices for Part D, ending the 2003 law's arrangement in which manufacturers set prices and the government is barred from interfering. Drug companies' interest in keeping prices high runs directly against beneficiaries' interest in paying less.

industries.industry: Private health insurers offering Part D drug plans
industries.note: A Medicare-operated plan with a uniform national $35 premium would have competed directly with private drug plans for enrollees, threatening their Part D business. Insurers' interest in keeping the market exclusive ran against beneficiaries getting a cheaper public option.
